lines: Welcome to Data Structures and Algorithms.
Before any structure, the language its costs are written in.
A claim like... quicksort is big O of n log n... hides three choices.
Which bound? Which case? And which resource?
Most arguments about complexity are really arguments about which one was meant.
All familiar? Swipe on.
Big O, big Omega, and Theta are inequalities.
Pick two constants, and a threshold... and the inequality must hold for every size past it.
Here, three n squared plus ten n sits between three n squared and four n squared... from ten onward.
When n is nine, the value is three hundred and thirty three. That is just above the line.
The constants can't depend on n. That's the whole trick.
The function two to the n plus one is in big O of the function two to the n. Double it, and you are done.
Now, is the function two to the two n in big O of two to the n?
answer: No. Two to the two n is four to the n... and dividing by two to the n leaves two to the n, which grows without bound.
So no constant works. An exponent multiplies the base. It isn't a constant factor.
Logarithm bases are different... they only differ by a constant.

lines: Little o means strictly slower.
For every constant c, f eventually falls below c times g.
When the ratio has a limit, zero means little o... a positive constant means Theta... and infinity means little omega.
But the limit may not exist. So the ratio test is sufficient... not necessary.
People say Big O means worst case. It does not, and the confusion costs real mistakes.
Two separate questions are hiding here. First, which input do you mean: the best, the typical, or the worst? That choice gives you one cost function.
Second, how does that function compare with a simple one like n squared? That comparison is the bound.

Insertion sort on eight items shows it: seven comparisons on sorted input, about nineteen on a random one, twenty eight reversed. Each case has its own exact growth rate, and either axis can be chosen freely.
Quicksort that always takes the first key as pivot does nearly half a million comparisons on a thousand keys that are already sorted.
Now let it choose the pivot by a coin flip instead. Same sorted input. What do you expect it to cost?
answer: About eleven thousand comparisons, and that holds for every input order, not just this one.
The average is a different promise. It averages over inputs, and it fails the moment real data stops looking like your assumption, sorted data being the classic case.
The expectation over the algorithm's own coins asks nothing of the input. The adversary picks the data, and the guarantee still holds.

lines: Two thousand runs, one thousand keys.
The mean is about eleven thousand. The slowest run, about fifteen and a half thousand.
An expectation allows rare slow runs.
With high probability bounds the tail instead... the chance of failure is at most one over n to the c, and you pick c.
A bigger c only costs a bigger constant.
Services are judged on tails. So ask which one you're being given.
Does a list of a thousand distinct numbers contain a duplicate?
Compare every pair... almost five hundred thousand steps, and no extra storage.
Heapsort in place, then one scan... about eighteen thousand.
Or a hash set... a thousand lookups, each fast only in expectation, but a thousand values stored.
Time bought with space. Always say which two resources, and what you count.
Asymptotics describe growth... not speed at one size.
A hundred n beats n squared only above a hundred.
Below that point, the slower algorithm in theory is the faster one in practice.
Where constants and cache effects decide, measure.
Here is a trap that fools people who know the notation well. Trial division tests a number by trying every divisor up to its square root.
For a thirty two bit prime that is about sixty five thousand tries. Give the number twice the bits and it needs over four billion.
The input grew by a factor of two, and the work grew by a factor of sixty five thousand. Measured in bits, which is what the input really occupies, that is exponential.
The name for it is pseudo-polynomial: fine in the value, terrible in the length.
Time for a feel for the ladder. Take a million items and a machine doing a billion steps a second.
A logarithmic algorithm needs a handful of steps; you will not notice it. Linearithmic takes a few hundredths of a second. Quadratic takes about a quarter of an hour.
An exponential one never finishes at this size: at sixty four items it already needs centuries.
But every one of those times quietly assumed that all steps cost the same. That assumption is what the rest of the course tests.
Seven things to keep.
Inequalities with witnesses. Strict little o and little omega. Bound is not case. Average is not expected.
High probability is a statement about the tail. Time can be traded for space. Constants rule small inputs. And for numbers, n means the size in bits.
So, quicksort is big O of n log n... is an upper bound on expected time, with random pivots.
With a fixed pivot, the worst case is Theta of n squared.
Next, the word RAM model... the machine behind those step counts.
